Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Working diagnosis and impressions: Migraine with aura (acute, first presentation) consistent with unilateral left-sided headache, visual aura, nausea/vomiting, and photophobia; no focal neurological deficits reported at this time.
- Relevant differential diagnoses (from DDx) and reasoning:
  - Migraine with aura — High likelihood: matches unilateral headache with visual disturbances and associated nausea.
  - Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) — Medium likelihood: sudden onset headache with vomiting and dizziness warrants consideration of a vascular catastrophe; no thunderclap description or neurologic deficits observed, but red flags present to monitor.
  - Ischemic stroke/TIA with visual symptoms — Medium likelihood: abrupt onset with visual disturbances and dizziness; absence of motor/sensory deficits lowers likelihood relative to migraine.
- Plan priorities: Symptom control for current migraine; assess with a full neurological exam if not improved; ensure patient education on warning signs that require urgent care.
- Notes on DDx alignment: Transcript supports migraine with aura as primary; DDx adds consideration of SAH and stroke as red flags to monitor if symptoms evolve.

Management Plan

- Immediate management and treatments provided/recommended:
  - Ibuprofen (NSAID) as a potential migraine treatment.
  - Antiemetic recommended to manage nausea.
  - Hydration and symptom relief suggestions: sugary, carbonated drinks (e.g., cola) to accompany treatment.
  - Advise rest and avoidance of screens during the episode.
  - If symptoms improve, the plan includes cancellation of the appointment; if not improved, proceed with a full neurological assessment today.
- Follow-up and monitoring:
  - Schedule/arrange an assessment today with potential full neurological exam if not improving.
  - Return or seek urgent care if symptoms worsen or new neurological signs develop.
- Patient education and expectations:
  - Migraines can improve within 30–60 minutes for some, but can last several hours; options exist to escalate to migraine-specific relief medications if needed.
  - Red flags to seek urgent care include sudden, "thunderclap" severe headache, new neurological deficits, neck stiffness, fever, or altered mental status.

- Migraine with aura

  - Justification: Unilateral left-headedness with visual aura (zigzag lines, blurred vision), nausea/vomiting, worsened by movement; female patient with family history of migraines supports susceptibility.
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Justification: Sudden onset headache with vomiting and dizziness; red flags present for potential vascular catastrophe; no thunderclap description or focal deficits yet.
- Ischemic stroke/TIA with visual symptoms
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Justification: Acute onset headache with visual disturbance and dizziness; absence of motor deficits lowers probability but stroke can present atypically.
